name: Ruth
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (in Brenton’s public-domain English translation) and the Dead Sea Scrolls fragments of Ruth (2QRuthᵃ, 2QRuthᵇ, 4QRuthᵃ, 4QRuthᵇ), which differ from the traditional Hebrew text only in small details. Where the written Hebrew text (ketiv) and the traditional reading (qere) differ, the translation follows the reading that makes sense in context and the footnotes give the other. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible, which agrees with the Hebrew in Ruth. Weights and measures are given in modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes.

verses.text: During the era when judges governed Israel, famine struck, and a man from Bethlehem{a} in Judah left with his wife and both sons, to reside as foreigners in Moabite territory.

The man’s name was Elimelech,{b} his wife’s was Naomi,{c} and his two sons were called Mahlon{d} and Chilion.{e} The family belonged to Ephrath, near Bethlehem in Judah. Having reached Moabite territory, they settled there.
Then Elimelech, Naomi’s husband, died, leaving her alone with her two sons.
Both sons married Moabite women. The first wife’s name was Orpah,{f} the second’s was Ruth.{g} After they had lived there some ten years,
Then Mahlon and Chilion both died as well, and the woman was left bereft, without her two boys or her husband.
Naomi prepared to leave Moab with her two daughters-in-law and head home, because word had reached her in Moab that Yahweh had turned his attention to his people and supplied them with bread.{h}
So she departed the place of her stay, accompanied by her two sons’ wives, and the three took the road back toward the land of Judah.
Naomi urged each of her daughters-in-law, “Go on back, both of you, to your own mothers’ homes. May Yahweh show faithful love{i} to you, just as you showed it to the departed and to me.
May Yahweh let each of you find peace in a new husband’s household!” She kissed them goodbye, but they began sobbing aloud.
They protested, “No, we are returning with you, to your people.”
Naomi replied, “Go home, my girls. Why come along with me? Am I still carrying sons in my body who could become your husbands?
Go home, my girls, and be on your way. I am too old to take a husband. Even supposing I had hope, and were married tonight, and gave birth to sons,
would you hold off until they were grown? Would you stay unmarried for their sake? Certainly not, my girls! My lot is far more bitter than yours, because Yahweh’s own hand has struck me down.”
Then they lifted up their voices and wept again. And Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her.
Naomi said, “See, your brother’s widow has gone home to her people and her gods. Follow her back.”

Ruth replied, “Do not press me to abandon you or to turn back from going with you. Wherever you travel, I will travel, and wherever you stay overnight, so will I. Your people will be mine, and your God will be my God.
Where you die, I die, and I will be laid in the ground beside you. May Yahweh punish me severely if anything other than death separates you and me.”
Seeing how firmly Ruth had resolved to accompany her, Naomi stopped arguing.
The two of them traveled on until they arrived in Bethlehem. Their arrival set the entire town buzzing, and the local women exclaimed, “Can this really be Naomi?”
She told them, “Don’t call me Naomi. Call me Mara,{j} because Shaddai{k} has embittered my life terribly.
I left here with plenty, but Yahweh has returned me with nothing. Why call me Naomi, now that Yahweh has stood as a witness against me{l} and Shaddai has sent disaster on me?”
That is how Naomi came back, along with Ruth, her Moabite daughter-in-law, who had come with her out of Moab. They reached Bethlehem just as the barley harvest was starting (in March–April).{m}

notes.text: Bethlehem means “house of bread.”
Elimelech means “my God is king.”
Naomi means “pleasant” or “my pleasantness.”
The meaning of Mahlon is uncertain; it is often explained as “sickly” or “weakness.”
Chilion probably means “failing,” “finished,” or “consumption.”
The meaning of Orpah is uncertain; it is often connected with ‘oref, “back of the neck,” as one who turned back (verse 14).
The meaning of Ruth is uncertain; it is often explained as “friend” or “companion,” or as “refreshment.”
Hebrew lehem, “bread,” echoing the name Bethlehem.
Hebrew hesed, “steadfast love, loyal kindness,” a key word in Ruth (2:20; 3:10).
Mara means “bitter.”
A divine name, traditionally translated “the Almighty”; its original meaning is uncertain. Also in verse 21. The Septuagint reads “the Mighty One.”
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint and some other ancient versions read “has humbled me,” from the same Hebrew letters with different vowels.

The barley harvest began around Passover in the first month of the spring-start calendar, Nisan (in March–April), and lasted about seven weeks until the wheat harvest ended at Pentecost/Shavuot (2:23). Today barley in this region is reaped mainly in April.

verses.text: Naomi had a kinsman through her husband, a man of standing{a} from Elimelech’s family, named Boaz.{b}
Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, “Allow me to go out into the fields and pick up leftover grain behind anyone who is kind enough to permit it.” Naomi answered, “Go ahead, my daughter.”
Off she went, and into a field, where she began collecting grain behind the harvesters. As it happened, the plot she chose belonged to Boaz, a member of Elimelech’s clan.
And look, Boaz came from Bethlehem. And he said to the reapers, “Yahweh be with you!” And they answered, “Yahweh bless you.”
Boaz asked the servant in charge of the harvesters, “Who is that young woman with you?”
The foreman answered, “She is a Moabite girl who came back along with Naomi from Moab.

She asked, ‘May I please follow the harvesters and collect fallen heads of grain among the bundles?’ She came, and from first thing this morning until just now she has stayed at it, pausing only briefly in the hut.”{c}
Boaz then spoke to Ruth: “Listen to me, my daughter. Don’t go off to gather in someone else’s field, and don’t move on from here. Stay right beside the young women who work for me.

Keep watch on the field where the men are cutting grain, and trail behind the women. I have ordered the young men to leave you alone. Whenever you are thirsty, walk over to the water jars and drink what the men have drawn.”
Ruth dropped with her face to the ground, bowing low, and asked him, “Why are you so generous, noticing me, when I am a foreigner?”{d}

Boaz answered, “Everything you have done for your husband’s mother since your husband died has been reported to me in full: how you abandoned your own father, your mother, and your homeland, to settle among a nation you had never known.
May Yahweh pay you back for your deeds, and may you receive full wages from Yahweh, the God of Israel, beneath whose wings{e} you have come for shelter.”
She responded, “May I always find such approval from you, sir. You have reassured me and spoken tenderly to your servant, though I do not even rank with your hired women.”

At mealtime Boaz invited her, “Join us here, help yourself to the bread, and dip a piece into the sour wine.” Ruth took her place next to the harvesters, and he passed her roasted kernels. She ate her fill and still had food left over.
When she got up to resume gathering, Boaz ordered his workers, “Even let her pick among the bundled stalks, and don’t embarrass her.
Even pull a few stalks out of the bundles and drop them for her to pick up. Don’t scold her.”
So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she beat out what she had gleaned, and it was about three-fifths of a bushel{f} of barley.
She lifted up what she had gathered and went back into town. Her husband’s mother saw how much she had collected. Ruth also took out the leftovers from her meal and handed them to Naomi.

Her mother-in-law asked, “Where did you gather grain today? Where were you working? A blessing on whoever noticed you!” Ruth described to her mother-in-law whose field she had worked in, and said, “The man I worked for today is named Boaz.”

Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, “May Yahweh bless him, for his loyal love has not left the living or the dead!” Then Naomi added, “That man is one of our close kinsmen, among those with the duty to redeem for our family.”{g}
Ruth the Moabite continued, “He also told me, ‘Stay with my workers until they have brought in my whole harvest.’”
Naomi told her daughter-in-law Ruth, “It is wise, my daughter, for you to work with his young women, so that no one harms you in a different field.”
So she stayed close to Boaz’s young women, gathering grain until both the barley and the wheat harvests were over (in May–June).{h} And she kept living with her mother-in-law.

notes.text: Or “a man of standing” or “a man of wealth”; Hebrew gibbor hayil. Compare “a worthy woman” (’eshet hayil) in 3:11.
The meaning of Boaz is uncertain; it is often explained as “in him is strength” or “quickness.” Boaz was also the name of one of the two bronze pillars of Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 7:21).
The meaning of the Hebrew of the last part of this verse is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “and she stood from morning until evening and has not rested in the field even a little.”
The Hebrew contains a pun: the verb “take notice” (hikkir) sounds like the word “foreigner” (nokriyyah).
Hebrew kanaf, “wing,” also “edge of a garment”; compare 3:9.
Hebrew “about an ephah”; an ephah was about 22 liters (L). That much threshed barley would weigh roughly 30 pounds (13–14 kilograms, kg), a remarkably large amount for one day’s gleaning.

Hebrew go’el (plural go’alim), the close relative who had the duty to buy back family land, to redeem a relative sold into slavery, to avenge a relative’s death, and, in Ruth, to provide an heir for the dead (Leviticus 25:25–55; Numbers 35:19; Deuteronomy 25:5–10). Also in 3:9, 12–13; 4:1–8, 14.
The barley harvest, beginning in March–April, was followed by the wheat harvest, which ended around Pentecost/Shavuot in the third month, Sivan (in May–June): about seven weeks in all.

verses.text: Her mother-in-law Naomi then said, “My daughter, should I not look for a secure home for you, where things will go well for you?
Boaz, whose women you worked beside, is our kinsman. Tonight he will be winnowing his barley on the threshing floor.
So bathe, put on perfume, dress in your best cloak,{a} and go to the threshing floor. Keep out of his sight until he has finished his meal and drink.
When he lies down, make a mental note of where he sleeps. Go there, lift the cover from his feet, and lie down. He will explain what you should do.”
Ruth told her, “Whatever you tell me,{b} I will carry out.”
She went down to the threshing floor and carried out all her mother-in-law’s instructions.
After Boaz had finished eating and drinking, and was in good spirits, he went to sleep beside the grain pile. She slipped in quietly, lifted the covering from his feet, and lay down.
In the middle of the night the man woke with a start, rolled over, and discovered a woman lying by his feet!
He said, “Who are you?” And she answered, “I am Ruth, your female servant. Spread your wing{c} over your female servant, for you are a family redeemer.”
He said, “Yahweh bless you, my daughter! This latest act of loyalty is even finer than your first, since you have not chased after the younger men, rich or poor.
Now, my daughter, have no fear. I will do everything you request, since everyone in my town’s gate{d} knows you are a woman of excellent character.
It is true that I am a kinsman-redeemer. Yet there is another man who is a nearer relative than I am.

Stay here for the night. In the morning, if he is willing to act as your redeemer, fine, let him do so. If he is unwilling, then I swear by the life of Yahweh that I will redeem you myself. Now sleep until morning.”
She slept by his feet till dawn, and got up while it was still too dark for anyone to make out a face. He said, “No one must find out that a woman visited the threshing floor.”
Then he said, “Hand me the cloak you have on, and hold it open.” She held it out, and he scooped in six measures{e} of barley, laying the load across her shoulders. Then she{f} returned to the town.
When she reached her mother-in-law, Naomi inquired, “How did things turn out, my daughter?” Ruth recounted everything the man had done for her,
and added, “These six measures of barley are his gift to me, because he told me,{g} ‘Do not go home to your mother-in-law with nothing.’”
Naomi answered, “Sit tight, my daughter, until you find out how things stand. The man will not relax until he has settled this affair today.”

notes.text: So the traditional reading (qere), “go down”; the written Hebrew text (ketiv) has “I will go down.” A similar difference occurs in verse 4 (“lie down”).
The traditional reading (qere) adds “to me.”
Hebrew kanaf, “wing” or “edge of a garment,” a request for marriage and protection; compare 2:12 and Ezekiel 16:8.
Hebrew “all the gate of my people.”

The Hebrew does not name the unit. Six ephahs would be far too heavy to carry; six seahs (about 4 bushels, 1 seah being about 7.3 liters) or six omers would be possible. The Septuagint reads “six measures.”
So most Hebrew manuscripts. Some Hebrew manuscripts, the Syriac, and the Latin Vulgate read “she.”
The traditional reading (qere) adds “to me”; the written Hebrew text (ketiv) lacks it.

verses.text: Meanwhile Boaz climbed to the town gate and seated himself there. Just then the redeemer he had mentioned walked past. Boaz called, “Come over, my friend,{a} and sit here.” So he came over and sat.
And he took ten men of the elders of the city and said, “Sit down here.” So they sat down.
He addressed the redeemer: “Naomi, who has returned from Moab, is putting up for sale the plot that belonged to our kinsman Elimelech.

I decided to bring it to your attention: purchase it before these people seated here and before my people’s elders. If you want to redeem it, do so. If you{b} don’t, tell me so that I know, because nobody else has the right to redeem it except you, and I am next after you.” He answered, “I will redeem it.”
Boaz continued, “On the day you acquire the land from Naomi, you also take on{c} Ruth the Moabite, the dead man’s widow, so that his name will be carried on with his inherited property.”
The redeemer answered, “Then I am unable to redeem it, since that could ruin my own estate. You exercise my redemption right yourself, because I cannot.”
In earlier days in Israel, this was how redemption and exchange were validated: one party removed his sandal and handed it to the other. That was the way of making a transaction official in Israel.
So when the redeemer told Boaz, “Purchase it yourself,” he took off his sandal.
Boaz addressed the elders and everyone present: “Today you are witnesses that I am buying from Naomi every possession of Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon.

I am also taking Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon’s widow, to be my wife, so that the dead man’s name will continue on his inherited land and not disappear from his family or from the records at his hometown’s gate. Today you are my witnesses.”

All the people gathered at the gate, along with the elders, answered, “We are witnesses! May Yahweh make the wife entering your home like Rachel and Leah, the two who together built the family of Israel. May you prosper in Ephrathah and gain fame in Bethlehem.
and may your family prosper like Perez’s, the son Tamar bore for Judah, through the children Yahweh gives you by this young woman.”
So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and Yahweh gave her conception, and she bore a son.
The women told Naomi, “Praise be to Yahweh, who has not left you today without a family redeemer! May the child’s name become famous throughout Israel!
He will restore your vitality and care for you when you are old, for he was born to your daughter-in-law. She loves you, and she has proven better to you than seven sons.”
Naomi picked up the baby, held him against her chest, and took care of him.
The neighbor women gave him his name, announcing, “Naomi has a son!” They called him Obed.{d} He would become Jesse’s father, and so David’s grandfather.
This is the genealogy of Perez. To Perez was born Hezron,
to Hezron was born Ram, to Ram was born Amminadab,
to Amminadab was born Nahshon, to Nahshon was born Salmah,{e}
Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed,
Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.

notes.text: Hebrew peloni almoni, “so-and-so,” an expression used when a name is withheld.
So many Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint, the Syriac, and the Latin Vulgate. The Hebrew text reads “if he.”

So the traditional reading (qere), the Septuagint, and the Latin Vulgate (“you acquire”). The written Hebrew text (ketiv) reads “I acquire.” The Hebrew text also reads “and from Ruth”; the translation follows a widely accepted correction, “also Ruth” (compare verse 10).
Obed means “servant” or “worshiper,” perhaps short for Obadiah, “servant of Yahweh.”
Hebrew Salmah; in verse 21 Salmon. The Septuagint has “Salmon” in both verses.
